PMH: HTN, controlled on lisinopril 10 mg daily. NKDA.
Diet: skips breakfast, fast food lunch 4x/wk, soda 2/day. Exercise: none, desk job. Sleeps ~6 hrs.

Vitals: BP 128/78, HR 74, wt 214 lb, ht 64 in, BMI 36.7.
Exam: obese, abd soft NT, lungs CTA, heart RRR. Knees no effusion, full ROM. No LE edema.

Class 2 obesity (BMI 36.7), HTN at goal.
Counseled >10 min: cut soda, add protein breakfast, portion control, goal loss 1-2 lb/wk.
Walk 10 min daily, build to 30 min 5x/wk.
Dietitian referral placed.
Continue lisinopril 10 mg daily.

summary: A 50-year-old female presented for weight-management counseling after a 15 lb weight gain over the last 2 years, with fatigue and knee aches with stairs. She denies chest pain, shortness of breath, polyuria and polydipsia. She has hypertension on lisinopril 10 mg daily, and her BMI is 36.7 with a normal A1c and TSH. The assessment was class 2 obesity with hypertension at goal. She received diet and exercise counseling and a dietitian referral, continues lisinopril, and will follow up in 6 weeks for a weight check.

Furosemide was increased to 40 mg BID with doses timed to her shifts, other medications continue, a repeat BMP is planned in 1 week, and nephrology follow-up is within 1 week.

The assessment was RSV bronchiolitis, mild to moderate, with adequate hydration. A trial of albuterol was stopped as ineffective, dextromethorphan cough syrup was discontinued, and acetaminophen was increased to 150 mg every 6 hours as needed. She went home with supportive care, return precautions, and a PCP recheck in 24-48 hours.

note: Rheumatology inpatient follow up dictation, hospital day 2, on a 75-year-old female admitted with an acute gout flare of the right first metatarsophalangeal joint. She flew home from overseas six days ago after a fourteen hour flight, ate rich meals and drank more wine than usual during the trip, and two days after arriving developed severe right big toe pain to the point that she could not bear weight and came to the emergency department. She denies fever, denies chills, denies any trauma to the foot, and denies calf pain or leg swelling, which mattered to check given the long flight. She has chronic kidney disease stage 3, hypertension, and one previous milder gout attack in the same toe years ago. Home medications on admission were hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily and amlodipine 5 mg daily. Vitals this morning are temperature 98.9 Fahrenheit, heart rate 84, blood pressure 142 over 82, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. On exam the right first MTP joint is warm, red, swollen and exquisitely tender with limited motion, the left foot is normal, and both calves are soft and nontender without asymmetry. Arthrocentesis yesterday showed needle shaped negatively birefringent crystals consistent with monosodium urate, synovial white count 18,000, and the gram stain and culture are negative so far. Serum uric acid was 9.4, creatinine 1.5 with an eGFR of 35, and the blood white count was 11.6. Impression is an acute gout flare, crystal proven, precipitated by travel, dietary indiscretion, dehydration and hydrochlorothiazide use, in the setting of chronic kidney disease stage 3. Because of her kidney function NSAIDs are avoided and colchicine is not preferred. She was started yesterday on prednisone 40 mg daily, correction, prednisone 30 mg daily for five days, with her pain improving from nine out of ten to four out of ten. Plan is to continue prednisone 30 mg daily, stop the hydrochlorothiazide and start losartan 25 mg daily instead for blood pressure and its mild uric acid lowering effect, continue amlodipine 5 mg daily, encourage oral hydration, and elevate the foot with ice. I will plan to start allopurinol 50 mg daily at rheumatology clinic follow up in two weeks once the flare has resolved, with a uric acid recheck after. Anticipate discharge tomorrow if the pain continues to improve and she is walking safely.

The impression is a crystal-proven acute gout flare in the setting of chronic kidney disease stage 3. Prednisone 30 mg daily is continued with improving pain, hydrochlorothiazide is replaced by losartan, and allopurinol is planned after the flare resolves.

note:
This is a pulmonology clinic follow-up visit for a 55-year-old female with pulmonary sarcoidosis, stage II on chest imaging, diagnosed about three years ago by endobronchial ultrasound lymph node biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas. She also has type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. Since her last visit she reports a persistent dry cough, exertional shortness of breath after one flight of stairs, and fatigue. She denies fever, night sweats, hemoptysis, chest pain, and eye redness or eye pain. She lives alone, has limited social support with no family nearby, and admits she has trouble keeping track of her pills and has missed some doses.

When asked about her prednisone she first told me she takes 10 mg daily, but after we reviewed the pill bottle she brought she is actually taking 20 mg daily, which is the dose prescribed at her last visit, so 20 mg daily is her correct current dose. She also takes metformin 500 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, and omeprazole 20 mg daily. On direct questioning she also buys over-the-counter supplements on her own, namely calcium carbonate 1200 mg daily, vitamin D3 5000 units daily, and echinacea capsules daily, which she started to protect her bones and boost her immunity while on steroids.

Vital signs today were blood pressure 134/82, heart rate 78, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air at rest. During a six-minute walk test she covered 380 meters and her saturation fell to 90%. She is comfortable and speaks in full sentences. Her lungs are clear to auscultation without wheeze or crackles. There is no erythema nodosum or other skin lesion. Her eyes show no conjunctival injection. Pulmonary function testing today showed FVC 74% of predicted, down from 80% a year ago, and DLCO 58% of predicted, down from 64%. Chest CT from last month shows stable bilateral perihilar lymphadenopathy and perilymphatic nodules without new fibrosis. Laboratory results today include serum calcium 10.9 mg/dL, which is mildly elevated, creatinine 0.9, and hemoglobin A1c 7.4%.

My impression is pulmonary sarcoidosis with a modest decline in lung function despite prednisone 20 mg daily, so she needs a steroid-sparing agent. Her mild hypercalcemia is most likely related to her calcium and vitamin D supplements in the setting of sarcoidosis, since granulomas increase production of active vitamin D. Her diabetes is above goal with an A1c of 7.4% on steroids, and her hypertension and reflux are stable.

I asked her to stop the calcium carbonate, vitamin D3, and echinacea today and explained why supplements can be harmful in sarcoidosis. I am starting methotrexate 10 mg once weekly with folic acid 1 mg daily after baseline CBC, liver tests, and hepatitis serologies, and I reviewed that methotrexate is taken once a week only and never daily. Prednisone stays at 20 mg daily for now. Metformin is increased from 500 mg twice daily to 1000 mg twice daily for her A1c. Lisinopril and omeprazole continue unchanged. Because she lives alone, I referred her to social work and asked the pharmacy to prepare weekly blister packs, and a nurse will call her in two weeks to check on medication use. We will repeat the serum calcium with a 24-hour urine calcium in two weeks and repeat pulmonary function tests in three months, and she should have an annual eye exam. She was told to call us for worsening breathlessness, fever, or chest pain, and she will return to clinic in six weeks.
summary: A 55-year-old female with pulmonary sarcoidosis, type 2 diabetes, hypertension and reflux has persistent dry cough, exertional shortness of breath and fatigue. She lives alone with limited social support and was found to be taking prednisone 20 mg daily plus self-purchased calcium carbonate, vitamin D3 and echinacea. Testing showed FVC down to 74% and DLCO 58% of predicted, desaturation to 90% on a six-minute walk, calcium 10.9 mg/dL and A1c 7.4%. The impression was sarcoidosis with modest functional decline, likely supplement-related mild hypercalcemia, and diabetes above goal. The supplements were stopped, methotrexate 10 mg weekly with folic acid was started, metformin was increased, and social work, pharmacy and nurse support were arranged.

note:
Hospital day 2 progress note for a 41-year-old male admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. A professional medical interpreter was used by video for the entire visit, and the patient confirmed his understanding through the interpreter. He reports that his fever and chills improved overnight, but he still has a productive cough with yellow sputum and right-sided pleuritic chest pain that is better than yesterday. He denies hemoptysis, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. He was weaned off supplemental oxygen yesterday afternoon and has needed none overnight. He is a current smoker of about half a pack per day and has no other medical history. He has no known drug allergies.

Current medications are ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, both started on admission, plus acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for fever.

Vital signs this morning are temperature 99.1 F, heart rate 88, blood pressure 124/76, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. He is comfortable and speaking in full sentences. On exam there are crackles with bronchial breath sounds at the right base. There is no wheezing. His heart rhythm is regular and his abdomen is soft and nontender. White blood cell count has improved from 15.2 on admission to 11.4 today, and creatinine is 0.9. The admission chest x-ray showed a right lower lobe consolidation. Blood cultures show no growth at 48 hours and the urine Legionella antigen was negative.

My assessment is community-acquired pneumonia that is clinically improving, with no oxygen requirement and no fever for 24 hours. I am stopping the IV ceftriaxone and starting amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg by mouth twice daily, and I am changing azithromycin to 500 mg by mouth once daily to complete 5 days in total. Acetaminophen continues as needed. I offered a nicotine patch 14 mg daily and smoking cessation counseling, and he accepted both through the interpreter. He will use an incentive spirometer. If he continues to do well, he can be discharged tomorrow with primary care follow-up in one week and a repeat chest x-ray in six weeks.
summary: A 41-year-old male, seen with a professional interpreter on hospital day 2 of admission for community-acquired pneumonia, reports improving fever and chills but persistent productive cough and pleuritic chest pain. He is now off oxygen with saturation 95% on room air, white blood cell count down from 15.2 to 11.4, and a right lower lobe consolidation on the admission chest x-ray. The assessment is clinically improving community-acquired pneumonia. Ceftriaxone is stopped, amoxicillin-clavulanate is started, azithromycin is changed to oral, and a nicotine patch is accepted. Discharge is anticipated tomorrow with primary care follow-up and a repeat chest x-ray in six weeks.

note:

Vitals: BP 146/84, HR 76, Temp 98.4 F, SpO2 97% RA.

R eye: diffuse conjunctival injection, mucopurulent discharge, crusted lids.
L eye: mild injection only.

A/P:

summary: An 83-year-old male presented to the ED with 2 days of right eye redness, yellow-green discharge with the eye matted shut in the morning, and a gritty feeling, and the left eye started itching today. He denies vision change, eye pain, photophobia, fever, sore throat and ear pain. Exam showed diffuse conjunctival injection with mucopurulent discharge on the right, mild injection on the left, no fluorescein uptake, and 20/30 acuity in each eye. The assessment was acute bacterial conjunctivitis of the right eye with early left eye involvement. He should call sooner or go to the emergency department if he cannot urinate, develops fever, or sees blood in his urine.

Pulmonology inpatient progress dictation, hospital day 3, on a 73-year-old female with interstitial lung disease admitted with acute on chronic hypoxemic respiratory failure. A professional interpreter was used for the entire visit by video, and everything below was confirmed with the patient through the interpreter. She has known fibrotic interstitial lung disease diagnosed about four years ago with a usual interstitial pneumonia pattern on high resolution CT, along with hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and recurrent urinary tract infections. She was admitted three days ago after a week of worsening shortness of breath and dry cough. She denies fever, chest pain, hemoptysis, and leg swelling. She has a documented allergy to sulfa drugs which causes a diffuse rash, so trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole is not an option for her.

Home medications were reviewed through the interpreter using her pill bottles. She takes prednisone 20 mg daily, correction, prednisone 10 mg daily, the bottle clearly says 10 mg, plus mycophenolate 500 mg twice daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily, and amlodipine 5 mg daily. She also takes nitrofurantoin 100 mg nightly to prevent urinary infections, which she has used for about two years.

On admission she was hypoxemic with oxygen saturation 86% on room air, improving to 93% on 4 liters nasal cannula. CT angiogram was negative for pulmonary embolism. High resolution CT showed her known basilar fibrosis with new bilateral ground glass opacities, consistent with an acute exacerbation. She received ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily for 2 days, which was stopped yesterday after the procalcitonin returned low and the blood cultures and respiratory viral panel were negative. She was started on methylprednisolone 60 mg IV every 12 hours on admission in place of her home prednisone. Today she says her breathing is slightly better.

Vitals today are temperature 37.0 Celsius, heart rate 92, blood pressure 98 over 60, respiratory rate 22, and oxygen saturation 93% on 3 liters, weaned from 4 liters. Labs show white count 13.1, creatinine 0.8, potassium 4.2, and glucose 168 on steroids. On exam she is comfortable at rest and speaking in short sentences, with bibasilar velcro crackles and digital clubbing. There is no wheezing. There is no peripheral edema.

Impression is acute exacerbation of fibrotic interstitial lung disease, slowly improving on high dose steroids. Her blood pressure runs low, so I am reducing amlodipine from 5 mg to 2.5 mg daily. I am stopping the nitrofurantoin because of the risk of pulmonary toxicity, and urology and her primary doctor will arrange another way to prevent urinary infections that avoids sulfa drugs. Because she is on high dose steroids and has a sulfa allergy, I am starting atovaquone 1500 mg daily for pneumocystis prophylaxis instead of trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole. Plan is to continue methylprednisolone 60 mg IV every 12 hours for now, continue mycophenolate 500 mg twice daily and omeprazole 20 mg daily, wean oxygen to keep saturation at or above 90%, start physical therapy, and repeat the metabolic panel and chest x-ray tomorrow. Discharge teaching will be done with a professional interpreter, and we will discuss goals of care and antifibrotic therapy with her at the next visit.

note:
Family medicine office dictation for a 52-year-old male with hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes, and hypertension, here to follow up on his cholesterol and discuss statin therapy. A professional medical interpreter was used by video for the whole visit. He reports mild fatigue lately and no other complaints. He denies chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, and leg pain with walking.

The main issue today is cost. He tells me the copays for his prescriptions add up every month, so he has been taking his atorvastatin only every other day, and he stopped ezetimibe 10 mg daily about three months ago to make his pills last. He first told me he takes atorvastatin 20 mg, but after reviewing the bottle with the interpreter, correction, it is atorvastatin 40 mg tablets, one tablet on the days that he takes it. He is also worried about statins because friends told him they damage the muscles and liver. He denies muscle aches, muscle weakness, dark urine, and abdominal pain when he does take the medication. His other medications are metformin 500 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, and amlodipine 5 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies.

Vitals today are blood pressure 136/84, heart rate 76, and weight 205 pounds with a BMI of 31. On exam there are no xanthomas, his heart is regular in rate and rhythm, lungs are clear, abdomen is obese and soft, and there is no leg edema with normal pedal pulses. Labs today show LDL 168, total cholesterol 242, HDL 38, triglycerides 210, hemoglobin A1c 7.8%, creatinine 0.9, and AST and ALT within normal limits. His estimated ten year cardiovascular risk is about 20 percent.

Assessment is hyperlipidemia with LDL well above goal, mainly because of cost related nonadherence rather than statin intolerance, in a patient with diabetes who is at high risk. His type 2 diabetes is above goal with an A1c of 7.8%, and his hypertension is near goal.

I spent about fifteen minutes through the interpreter explaining the benefits and safety of statins and the plan, and he agreed to take atorvastatin 40 mg once daily, every single day. Ezetimibe stays stopped for now and we will reconsider it if the repeat LDL is still above goal. Metformin is increased from 500 mg twice daily to 1000 mg twice daily. Lisinopril 20 mg daily and amlodipine 5 mg daily continue unchanged. I am referring him to the clinic pharmacist and social worker for help with medication costs, and I will switch his prescriptions to 90 day supplies at a discount generic program. Repeat a fasting lipid panel and ALT in eight weeks, and see him back in three months with an A1c. Dietary counseling was given, and he should call us sooner for muscle pain or dark urine.

note:
This is a hospital ward progress note for a 47-year-old female with type 1 diabetes on an insulin pump with continuous glucose monitoring, admitted overnight after a severe hypoglycemic episode in which she became confused and her husband gave glucagon 1 mg IM before EMS arrived. Her point-of-care glucose on arrival was 38 mg/dL, and she recovered fully after treatment in the emergency department. She reports frequent lows over the past month, mostly between 2 and 4 in the morning, and she often does not feel them coming on. She denies seizure, loss of consciousness, chest pain, and fever. Her insulin is lispro delivered by pump, and her A1c is 6.2%. The pump download shows an overnight basal rate of 0.9 units/hr, and the glucose monitor shows 6% of time below 54 mg/dL. Vitals this morning are blood pressure 118/70, heart rate 78, and temperature 98.2 F. She is alert and oriented with a nonfocal neurologic exam.

My impression is type 1 diabetes with recurrent hypoglycemia and hypoglycemia unawareness, related to overly tight control and an overnight basal rate that is too high. Plan is to lower the overnight basal rate from 0.9 to 0.7 units/hr, raise her glucose target to 110 mg/dL, and set the monitor low alert at 80 mg/dL. She will see the diabetes educator before discharge and in endocrinology clinic in 2 weeks, and her husband will be re-taught how to use glucagon.
